subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6! In this unit you become a statistician – someone who asks good questions, collects data carefully, organises it, and reads the story hidden inside the numbers. Statistics is everywhere. When a shopkeeper in the Hargeisa market works out the most popular size of sambusa to prepare each morning, when a health worker in Garissa studies how many children were vaccinated this year, or when Yusuf compares the goals his favourite football team scored across a season, they are all doing statistics.

outcomes: Tell the difference between a statistical question and a non-statistical question, and plan an investigation to answer one.
Classify data as categorical or numerical, and numerical data as discrete or continuous.
Choose a sensible way to collect data, understand population and sample, and recognise bias.
Organise raw data into frequency tables, including grouped and two-way tables.
Draw and read bar charts, pictograms, pie charts, line graphs and stem-and-leaf diagrams.
Calculate the three averages – mean, median and mode – and the range, and know when each average is most useful.
Interpret data, compare two sets of data, spot misleading graphs, and write valid conclusions.
Explain how the size of a sample affects how reliable and representative it is, weighing this against the time and cost of collecting more data.
Draw and read dual (compound) bar charts that show two or more data sets side by side for comparison.
Sort and record data using a Venn diagram (overlapping sets) and a Carroll diagram (a criteria grid), reading values from both.
Plot a scatter graph from paired data and describe the pattern as a positive, negative or no correlation between the two variables.
Read and construct a waffle diagram to show a percentage or proportion, and interpret data presented within an infographic.

concepts.title: Statistical Questions and the Investigation Cycle
concepts.explanation:
Statistics begins with a good question. A statistical question is one that you answer by collecting data, and where you expect the answers to vary. Compare these two questions: “How old is Farah?” has one fixed answer – it is not statistical. But “How old are the students in Year 7 at our school?” expects a variety of answers, and you can only answer it by collecting data. That makes it a statistical question.

Here are more examples so the difference becomes clear:

Statistical: “What is the most popular sport among Year 7 students?” (answers vary)

Statistical: “How many cups of camel milk does each family in the village drink per day?” (answers vary)

Not statistical: “How many days are in a week?” (one fixed answer: 7)

Not statistical: “What is the distance from Mogadishu to Kismaayo?” (one fixed answer)

Once you have a statistical question, you follow a clear path called the statistical investigation cycle. It has five stages, and good statisticians follow them every time:

Formulate a clear statistical question and predict what you might find.

Collect the data using a fair, planned method.

Organise the data into tables and charts.

Analyse the data by calculating averages and the range, and reading the charts.

Conclude by answering your original question honestly, and noting any limitations.

Before collecting data, statisticians often make a prediction (sometimes called a hypothesis). For example, Amina might predict, “I think most Year 7 students walk to school.” A prediction is not cheating – it helps focus the investigation and gives you something to test. Sometimes the data supports your prediction, and sometimes it surprises you. Both outcomes are useful, because both teach you something true about the world.
concepts.example: A well-formed statistical question is clear, specific and fair. “Are students healthy?” is too vague – what does *healthy* mean, and which students? A better version is, “How many hours of physical activity do Year 7 students at Nuur Academy do in a typical week?” This version is measurable, focused, and does not push people towards a particular answer. Learning to sharpen a vague question into a clear one is a real statistical skill.

concepts.title: Types of Data
concepts.explanation:
Before you collect or organise data, you must know what type of data it is, because the type decides which tables, charts and averages you can use. There are two big families: categorical and numerical.

Categorical data (also called qualitative data) sorts things into groups or names. You cannot do sensible arithmetic with it. Examples include favourite colour, type of livestock (camel, goat, cattle), method of travel to school, and nationality. You can count how many fall into each group, but you cannot find an “average colour.”

Numerical data (also called quantitative data) is made of numbers you can measure or count, and you *can* do arithmetic with it. Examples include age, height, number of siblings, and test scores. Numerical data splits further into two kinds:

Discrete data takes separate, countable values – usually whole numbers with gaps between them. You cannot have half of one. Examples: the number of goals scored, the number of goats in a herd, shoe size. You can count it.

Continuous data can take any value within a range and is found by measuring. Between any two values there is always another. Examples: height, mass, time, temperature, the distance to the masjid. You measure it, and the precision depends only on your instrument.

A quick test: *can you count it or must you measure it?* If Hassan counts 4 goats, that is discrete – there is no such thing as 4.5 goats in a count. If Hassan measures a goat’s mass as 32.6 kg, that is continuous – with a better scale he could measure 32.63 kg. Number of children is discrete; the time to walk to school is continuous.
concepts.example: There is one more useful pairing. Primary data is data you collect yourself, first-hand, for your own investigation – for example, by surveying your own class. Secondary data is data someone else collected, which you then use – for example, figures from a government census or a sports website. Primary data fits your exact question but takes time to gather; secondary data is quick to obtain but may not match your needs exactly. Knowing which you are using helps you judge how much to trust it.

concepts.title: Collecting Data – Samples and Bias
concepts.explanation: Imagine you want to know the favourite sport of every Year 7 student in a large city. Asking every single one would take far too long. Instead, statisticians study a sample – a smaller group chosen from the whole population – and use it to learn about everyone. The population is the entire group you are interested in; the sample is the part you actually collect data from. The most important idea in sampling is that a sample must be representative – it must fairly reflect the whole population. If your sample is… The size of a sample matters as much as how it is chosen. A larger sample usually gives a more reliable, more representative picture of the population, because a few unusual answers get 'averaged out' by all the typical ones. A very small sample can be misleading – if you ask just 3 students their favourite subject, one unusual answer can swing the whole result. But bigger samples take more time, cost more, and are not always possible, so real investigations balance reliability against the time and resources available.

concepts.title: Organising Data with Frequency Tables
concepts.explanation:
Raw data, straight from collection, is usually a messy list. A frequency table organises it so patterns become visible. Frequency simply means *how many times* a value appears. Often we build the table using a tally, marking one stroke for each item and crossing the fifth to make counting easy, then writing the total as the frequency.

Here is a simple frequency table. Aisha asked 50 students at Nuur Academy their favourite school subject:

The percentage column shows the proportion in each group. To find it, divide the frequency by the total and multiply by 100. For Science: 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%. The percentages always add up to 100%, which is a handy way to check your work. Percentages let you compare fairly even when totals differ.

When numerical data has many different values – especially continuous data – a simple table would be too long. Instead we use a grouped frequency table, sorting the data into equal class intervals. Here are the heights of 50 students:

When you build a grouped table, follow three rules: use equal intervals where possible (here each is 10 cm wide); make sure the groups do not overlap (use 140–149 then 150–159, never 140–150 then 150–160, or where would 150 go?); and make sure every value fits into exactly one group. The most common group – here 160–169 with 18 students – is called the modal class.

A two-way table shows two categorical variables at once. This one shows favourite subject split by gender:
concepts.example: Read a two-way table by finding where a row meets a column. How many girls chose Art? Find the Girls row and the Art column: 7. The totals row and total column let you check everything: the four subject totals (12 + 15 + 8 + 9) add to 44, and the two gender totals (23 + 21) also add to 44. If they did not match, you would know a mistake had slipped in.

concepts.title: Charts and Graphs
concepts.explanation: A good chart lets the eye see a pattern instantly. The skill is choosing the right chart for the type of data. Here are the ones you need in Year 7. Bar charts display categorical data using bars of equal width, with a gap between each bar because the categories are separate. The height of each bar shows its frequency. Always give the chart a title and label both axes. Bar charts are perfect for comparing groups, such as favourite sports or sales by product. A pictogram does the same job using pictures, where one… When you want to compare two or more data sets side by side for the same categories, use a dual (or compound) bar chart. Instead of one bar per category, you draw two or more bars, usually in different colours with a key, next to each other for every category – for example, boys' and girls' favourite sports drawn as paired bars for each sport.
concepts.example: Pie charts show how a whole is divided into parts. Each slice is a fraction of the full circle, and all the slices together make 360°. To find the angle for a slice, use: angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. Pie charts work best with a small number of categories and when you want to emphasise proportions rather than exact counts. For the favourite-subject data, Science (15 out of 50) needs an angle of 15 ÷ 50 × 360° = 108°.

concepts.title: Averages and Range
concepts.explanation:
An average is a single value that stands for a whole set of data – a “typical” value. There are three different averages, and a good statistician knows all three and when to use each. There is also the range, which measures how spread out the data is.

The mean is what most people call “the average.” To find it, add up all the values, then divide by how many values there are. Suppose a Kismaayo football team scored these goals in 9 matches: 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1, 3. The total is 2 + 0 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 18, and there are 9 matches, so the mean is 18 ÷ 9 = 2 goals per match. The mean uses every value, which is its strength – but that is also its weakness, because one very large or very small value can pull it off.

The median is the middle value once the data is placed in order. Using the ordered goals 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, there are 9 values, so the middle one is the 5th: the median is 2. If there is an even number of values, there are two middle values, and the median is the number halfway between them (their mean). For 4, 6, 8, 10 the two middle values are 6 and 8, so the median is (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7. The median is not affected by a single extreme value, which makes it very useful.

The mode is the value that appears most often. In the goals data, 2 appears three times – more than any other – so the mode is 2. Data can have more than one mode if two values tie (this is called bimodal), or no mode at all if every value appears once. The mode is the only average you can use with categorical data: the mode of a set of favourite subjects is simply the most popular subject.

The range is not an average – it measures spread. To find it, subtract the lowest value from the highest: range = highest − lowest. For the goals, the highest is 4 and the lowest is 0, so the range is 4 − 0 = 4. A small range means the data is consistent and bunched together; a large range means it is spread out and variable. The range and an average work together: the average tells you the *typical* value, and the range tells you *how much the values vary*.

Which average should you use? It depends on the data:

Use the mean when the data is fairly even with no extreme values – it uses all the information.

Use the median when there is an outlier (an unusually high or low value) that would distort the mean.

Use the mode for categorical data, or to find the single most common value.

Here is why outliers matter. A small shop records daily customers for a week: 45, 52, 48, 150, 49, 51, 47. The value 150 is an outlier – perhaps a festival day. The mean is (45 + 52 + 48 + 150 + 49 + 51 + 47) ÷ 7 = 442 ÷ 7 ≈ 63.1, but that is higher than almost every ordinary day. The median, the middle of the ordered list 45, 47, 48, 49, 51, 52, 150, is 49, which represents a typical day far better. This is exactly why the median is often the fairer choice.

You can also find the mean from a frequency table. Suppose 20 families reported how many children they have:
concepts.example: To find the mean, multiply each value by its frequency (that is the third column), add those products to get the grand total of children (38), then divide by the total number of families (20). The mean is 38 ÷ 20 = 1.9 children per family. Notice the mean does not have to be a whole number, even though you cannot have 1.9 children – it is a *typical* value, not a real family.

concepts.title: Venn Diagrams and Carroll Diagrams
concepts.explanation: Some data needs to be sorted by more than one property at once, and Venn and Carroll diagrams are two clear ways to do it. A Venn diagram uses overlapping circles inside a rectangle (the rectangle represents the whole population, sometimes called the universal set). Each circle stands for one property. Anything with both properties goes in the overlap; anything with neither goes outside both circles but inside the rectangle. For example, draw one circle for 'plays football' and one circle for 'plays basketball'. A student who plays both sports goes in the overlapping region; a student who plays neither goes outside both circles. A Carroll diagram does the same sorting job using a grid instead of circles. Each row and column is labelled with a property and its opposite (for example 'plays football' / 'does not play football' across the top, and 'plays basketball' / 'does not play basketball' down the side), and every student is placed in exactly one of the four boxes.
concepts.example: Suppose 30 students are asked whether they play football and whether they play basketball: 12 play both, 8 play only football, 6 play only basketball, and 4 play neither. In a Venn diagram, the overlap of the two circles holds 12, the football circle (outside the overlap) holds 8, the basketball circle (outside the overlap) holds 6, and the region outside both circles holds 4. Check the total: 12 + 8 + 6 + 4 = 30, which matches the number of students asked. The same information in a Carroll diagram would show 12 in the 'football AND basketball' box, 8 in 'football AND not basketball', 6 in 'not football AND basketball', and 4 in 'not football AND not basketball'.

concepts.title: Scatter Graphs
concepts.explanation: A scatter graph is used when you have two numerical measurements for the same set of items, and you want to see whether they are connected. Each item gives one point, plotted using one measurement as the x-value and the other as the y-value – for example, each student contributes one point using their hours of revision as x and their test score as y. Once every point is plotted, look at the overall pattern the points make. If the points drift upward from left to right, that is a positive correlation – as one quantity increases, so does the other (more revision, higher scores). If the points drift downward from left to right, that is a negative correlation – as one quantity increases, the other decreases (more hours watching television, lower scores, perhaps). If the points are scattered with no clear pattern, there is no correlation, and the two quantities are not linked in an obvious way.
concepts.example: A PE teacher records the age (in years) and the standing jump distance (in cm) of 8 students: (11, 120), (12, 128), (11, 118), (13, 135), (12, 125), (14, 140), (13, 132), (12, 126). Plotting age on the x-axis and jump distance on the y-axis, the points climb steadily from bottom-left to top-right, showing a positive correlation – older students in this group tend to jump further. Note that a scatter graph shows a correlation, a link between the two things; it does not by itself prove that one thing directly causes the other.

concepts.title: Waffle Diagrams and Infographics
concepts.explanation: A waffle diagram is a square grid of 100 small squares, arranged 10 by 10, used to show a percentage or proportion at a glance – it is the same 'hundred grid' picture used to explain what a percentage means. To show 37%, shade 37 of the 100 squares; the shaded fraction of the grid is instantly visible, which makes waffle diagrams useful for comparing two or three proportions side by side, such as the percentage of households in three villages with access to clean water. An infographic combines several elements – short pieces of text, icons, numbers and small charts (bar charts, pie charts, waffle diagrams and so on) – on a single page to tell a data story quickly, the way a poster or a news website might. Infographics are common in the real world, so it is an important skill to read one critically: check that each chart has a title and labelled axes or a key, check that the scale is not stretched or squashed to exaggerate a difference, and check whether the numbers shown actually support the headline claim.
concepts.example: A health poster uses a waffle diagram to show that 64 out of 100 people in a survey wash their hands before eating – 64 of the 100 small squares are shaded. The same poster might also include an infographic strip with an icon of a hand, the bold number '64%', and a short sentence explaining the survey size, combining the waffle diagram with icons and text to communicate the finding quickly.

methods.title: How to find the median
steps: Put all the values in order from smallest to largest.
If there is an odd number of values, the median is the middle one.
If there is an even number, the median is halfway between the two middle values (add them and divide by 2).

methods.title: How to find the mean from a frequency table
methods.example: The number of goals scored in 10 matches: 0 goals in 2 matches, 1 goal in 4 matches, 2 goals in 3 matches, 3 goals in 1 match. Find the mean.
steps: Multiply each value by its frequency.
Add up all those products to get the grand total.
Add up the frequencies to get how many values there are.
Divide the grand total by the number of values.

methods.title: How to choose the best average
methods.example: Find the mean, median and mode of: 3, 7, 5, 9, 5, 8, 6, 5, 4.
steps: Use the mean for even data with no extreme values.
Use the median when there is an outlier.
Use the mode for categorical data or the most common value.

methods.title: The range and consistency
methods.example: Two classes have the same mean of 85. Class A scored 78, 82, 85, 88, 92; Class B scored 65, 70, 85, 95, 100. Which class was more consistent?
steps: Solution: Range of A = 92 − 78 = 14.
Range of B = 100 − 65 = 35.
A smaller range means less variation, so Class A was more consistent, even though both classes have the same mean.
This shows why the range matters as well as the average.

methods.title: Mean or median?
methods.example: A shop’s daily customers for a week were 45, 52, 48, 150, 49, 51, 47. Should the owner use the mean or the median to describe a typical day?
steps: Solution: The value 150 is an outlier — much higher than the rest of the week's figures.
The mean is 442 ÷ 7 ≈ 63.1, which is higher than six of the seven days.
Ordering the data (45, 47, 48, 49, 51, 52, 150) shows the median is 49, much closer to most days.
Use the median instead of the mean whenever the data has an outlier.

methods.title: Pie chart angles
methods.example: 40 students named a favourite sport: Football 20, Basketball 8, Volleyball 6, Swimming 6. Find the angle for each slice of a pie chart.
steps: Solution: Angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°.
Basketball = 8 ÷ 40 × 360° = 72°.
Volleyball = 6 ÷ 40 × 360° = 54°.
Check: 180° + 72° + 54° + 54° = 360° — a full circle, so the answer is correct.

workedExamples.title: Statistical or not?
workedExamples.prompt: Decide which of these is a statistical question: (a) “How tall is Ibrahim?” (b) “How tall are the students in Year 7?”
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Question (a) has a single fixed answer – one measurement – so it is not statistical. Question (b) expects a variety of heights and can only be answered by collecting data from many students, so (b) is the statistical question.

workedExamples.title: Classify the data
workedExamples.prompt: Classify each as categorical, discrete numerical, or continuous numerical: (a) number of pets, (b) type of transport to school, (c) time to run 100 m, (d) shoe size.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: (a) You count pets in whole numbers, so discrete numerical. (b) Walk, bus, car… these are groups, so categorical. (c) Time is measured and can be any value like 14.7 s, so continuous numerical. (d) Shoe sizes come in fixed steps you count, so discrete numerical.

workedExamples.title: Find the mean, median and mode
workedExamples.prompt: Find the mean, median and mode of: 3, 7, 5, 9, 5, 8, 6, 5, 4.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Add them: 3 + 7 + 5 + 9 + 5 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 52. There are 9 values, so the mean = 52 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.8. Order the data: 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. The middle (5th) value is the median = 5. The value 5 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode = 5.

workedExamples.title: Pie chart angles
workedExamples.prompt: 40 students named a favourite sport: Football 20, Basketball 8, Volleyball 6, Swimming 6. Find the angle for each slice of a pie chart.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. Football = 20 ÷ 40 × 360° = 180°. Basketball = 8 ÷ 40 × 360° = 72°. Volleyball = 6 ÷ 40 × 360° = 54°. Swimming = 6 ÷ 40 × 360° = 54°. Check: 180 + 72 + 54 + 54 = 360°. The angles add to a full circle, so it is correct.

workedExamples.title: Mean from a frequency table
workedExamples.prompt: The number of goals scored in 10 matches: 0 goals in 2 matches, 1 goal in 4 matches, 2 goals in 3 matches, 3 goals in 1 match. Find the mean.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Multiply each value by its frequency: (0×2) + (1×4) + (2×3) + (3×1) = 0 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 goals. The number of matches is 2 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 10. So the mean = 13 ÷ 10 = 1.3 goals per match.

workedExamples.prompt: Using the two-way table from Concept 4, how many students in total chose Science, and how many girls chose English?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Find the Science column total: 15 students chose Science. Find where the Girls row meets the English column: 5 girls chose English. Reading a two-way table is just finding where a row meets a column.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: The mean of six numbers is 15. Five of them are 12, 14, 16, 18 and 11. Find the sixth number.
workedExamples.solution: Sum of all six numbers = 15 × 6 = 90. Sum of the five known numbers = 12 + 14 + 16 + 18 + 11 = 71. Sixth number = 90 − 71 = 19.

activities.title: Your Own Household Survey
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and family members to ask.
steps: Choose a statistical question, such as “How many cups of tea does each person drink in a day?”
Collect the data from at least six people and record it in a tally chart.
Turn your tally into a frequency table.
Work out the mean, median, mode and range of your data.
Write one honest sentence saying what a typical answer was and how much the answers varied.

activities.title: The Averages Card Game
activities.materials: number cards or paper slips numbered 1 to 20.
steps: Shuffle and deal five cards to yourself.
Find the mean, median, mode (if any) and range of your five numbers.
Deal five to a partner and compare whose set has the bigger mean and whose has the bigger range — or, if no partner is available, deal yourself a second hand and compare the two yourself.
Play several rounds and keep score of who wins each measure.
This game makes calculating averages fast and automatic.

activities.title: Market Price Investigation
activities.materials: the prices of one item (for example, a mango) from several stalls or shops.
steps: Collect the price of the same item from at least five different sellers.
Record the prices and find the mean price and the range.
The range tells you how much prices vary between sellers – is it large or small?
Write a short conclusion: where is the best value, and how spread out are the prices?

activities.title: Spot the Misleading Graph
activities.materials: newspapers, adverts, or packaging that show charts.
steps: Find any bar chart or graph in an advert or newspaper.
Check the vertical axis – does it start at zero, or somewhere higher?
Decide whether the graph makes a difference look bigger than it really is.
Redraw it fairly with the axis starting at zero and compare the two pictures.

activities.title: Pie Chart from Real Data (Family Task)
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and (if you have one) a protractor; a bowl of mixed items such as dates, stones and beans.
steps: Sort your items into groups and count how many are in each group.
Find the total, then work out each slice angle: (group ÷ total) × 360°.
Check your angles add up to 360°.
Draw the pie chart and label each slice. Explain which group is the largest.

activities.title: Consistency Challenge (Investigation)
activities.materials: a small ball or scrunched paper and a target, or a way to time an activity.
steps: Throw at the target ten times and record how many hits you get in sets of, say, five throws – or time yourself doing a task ten times.
Calculate the mean and the range of your results.
Practise, then repeat. Did your mean improve? Did your range get smaller (more consistent)?
Write about which changed more: your average performance or your consistency.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand averages best? When did the range tell you something the average could not? Where did you spot bias or a misleading graph? Share your answers with your teacher, a family member, or your AI tutor.

rules.title: Chart Labelling Rule
rules.text: The golden rule of every chart is: label everything. A chart without a title and axis labels is a puzzle no one can read. Choosing the wrong chart type – such as a pie chart for data that is not parts of a whole – confuses your reader instead of helping them.

rules.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
rules.text: Be careful about correlation and causation. Two things can rise together without one causing the other. In hot weather, both ice-cream sales and swimming accidents go up – they are correlated – but ice cream does not cause the accidents; the hot weather affects both. The rule to remember is: correlation does not prove causation. Just because two sets of numbers move together does not mean one makes the other happen.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Charts and Graphs.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A good chart lets the eye see a pattern instantly. The skill is choosing the right chart for the type of data. Here are the ones you need in Year 7.

Bar charts display categorical data using bars of equal width, with a gap between each bar because the categories are separate. The height of each bar shows its frequency. Always give the chart a title and label both axes. Bar charts are perfect for comparing groups, such as favourite sports or sales by product. A pictogram does the same job using pictures, where one symbol stands for a fixed number of items (for example, one goat symbol = 5 goats), so you must always read the key.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Averages and Range.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
An average is a single value that stands for a whole set of data – a “typical” value. There are three different averages, and a good statistician knows all three and when to use each. There is also the range, which measures how spread out the data is.

The mean is what most people call “the average.” To find it, add up all the values, then divide by how many values there are. Suppose a Kismaayo football team scored these goals in 9 matches: 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1, 3. The total is 2 + 0 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 18, and there are 9 matches, so the mean is 18 ÷ 9 = 2 goals per match. The mean uses every value, which is its strength – but that is also its weakness, because one very large or very small value can pull it off.

selfAssessment: I can tell the difference between a statistical question and a non-statistical question, and plan an investigation to answer one.
I can classify data as categorical or numerical, and numerical data as discrete or continuous.
I can choose a sensible way to collect data, understand population and sample, and recognise bias.
I can organise raw data into frequency tables, including grouped and two-way tables.
I can draw and read bar charts, pictograms, pie charts, line graphs and stem-and-leaf diagrams.
I can calculate the three averages – mean, median and mode – and the range, and know when each average is most useful.
I can interpret data, compare two sets of data, spot misleading graphs, and write valid conclusions.
